question: What is the main goal when medical help arrives immediately after a disaster?

options.A: To minimize death and illness
options.B: To train local volunteers
options.C: To rebuild damaged hospitals
options.D: To document insurance claims

explanation: You've got this! When disaster strikes, the immediate focus is always on saving lives and stopping severe illness through quick medical action.

question: Why do nurses have to change how they normally work when responding to a field disaster?

options.A: Basic utilities and sterile spaces are usually missing
options.B: Patients refuse standard medications in the field
options.C: Disaster protocols completely forbid using medications
options.D: Physicians are rarely present during emergencies

explanation: Great thinking! Out in the field, you won't find normal hospital comforts like constant running water or steady electricity, so nurses have to adapt cleverly and safely.

question: In a mass casualty incident, what does a RED triage tag mean?

options.A: Minor injuries that can wait until the end of the shift
options.B: Immediate life-threatening injuries with a high chance of survival
options.C: Injuries so severe that survival is unlikely
options.D: Deceased patients who need no further attention

explanation: Spot on! Red means urgent. It tells us the patient has a life-threatening problem that we can fix right now to save their life.

question: A patient in a disaster zone has a severe head injury, is unresponsive, breathing irregularly, and has no pulse. Which triage category fits best?

options.A: Red
options.B: Black
options.C: Yellow
options.D: Green

explanation: You're doing great. A black tag (or expectant) is used for catastrophic injuries where survival is sadly very unlikely, helping us save resources for those we can help.

question: What is the absolute first thing a nurse checks during an initial trauma assessment?

options.A: Pain assessment
options.B: Airway management
options.C: Wound dressing
options.D: Checking blood pressure

explanation: Think ABCs! Keeping the airway open is always step one because a blocked airway causes a patient to deteriorate the fastest.

question: Why is stopping heavy bleeding such a high priority in disaster trauma care?

options.A: Clean bandages are always in short supply
options.B: Blood spills make the clinical environment too slippery
options.C: Patients feel less pain if bleeding stops right away
options.D: Unchecked hemorrhage quickly leads to fatal hemorrhagic shock

explanation: Spot on! Uncontrolled bleeding causes blood pressure to crash rapidly, which can quickly become fatal if we don't jump in fast.

question: Where is the best spot to set up a temporary disaster field hospital?

options.A: Directly inside an unstable damaged building
options.B: In the deepest part of the flooded zone
options.C: As far away from the disaster victims as possible
options.D: On stable, accessible ground away from immediate hazards

explanation: Makes total sense! We want a safe, solid spot that ambulances and walking patients can easily reach without getting caught in secondary dangers.

question: Why is proper waste disposal so important right from the start in a field hospital?

options.A: To make the area look neat for visiting leaders
options.B: To comply with local parking regulations
options.C: To prevent secondary disease outbreaks in the camp
options.D: To ensure the medical tents do not blow away

explanation: You got it! Leftover medical and human waste quickly breeds harmful germs, turning the camp into a new sick zone if we aren't careful.

question: What is a major danger when a trapped victim is finally freed from a prolonged crush injury?

options.A: Crush syndrome and acute kidney failure
options.B: Immediate high blood pressure spikes
options.C: Sudden permanent blindness
options.D: Instantaneous bone hardening

explanation: Brilliant! When crushed muscles are released, they dump toxins like potassium and myoglobin into the blood, which can overwhelm and shut down the kidneys.

question: Why are IV fluids given to a patient with a severe crush injury before they are freed?

options.A: To prevent external skin infections
options.B: To numb the pain of broken bones
options.C: To make the patient sleep through the rescue
options.D: To flush out toxins and protect the kidneys

explanation: That's right! Pumping in fluids helps dilute and flush those nasty muscle toxins through the kidneys safely before they can cause severe damage.

question: Which type of illness spreads the fastest in crowded, poorly sanitized relief camps?

options.A: Degenerative joint diseases
options.B: Chronic autoimmune conditions
options.C: Waterborne infectious diseases
options.D: Hereditary metabolic disorders

explanation: Spot on! When clean water and toilets break down, infections like cholera and dysentery spread through the camp like wildfire.

question: What is your first nursing action if a patient in a relief camp presents with severe watery diarrhea?

options.A: Prescribe heavy exercise to boost immunity
options.B: Send the patient home immediately
options.C: Restrict all fluid intake to rest the bowel
options.D: Isolate the patient and initiate rehydration therapy

explanation: You're on the right track! Isolating stops it from spreading to others, while rehydration replaces all those lost body fluids immediately.

question: What is the main focus of Psychological First Aid (PFA) in a disaster?

options.A: Providing humane practical support and reducing distress
options.B: Conducting formal psychoanalysis sessions
options.C: Prescribing strong antidepressant medications
options.D: Diagnosing deep psychiatric disorders

explanation: Well done! PFA isn't about heavy therapy or psychoanalysis; it's about being human, offering practical comfort, and helping people feel safe.

question: Why must disaster nurses actively watch out for compassion fatigue and practice self-care?

options.A: Patients will lose respect for nurses who show emotion
options.B: Nurses are immune to stress if they work fast enough
options.C: Hospital managers require daily wellness logs from every nurse
options.D: Prolonged exposure to trauma can lead to severe emotional burnout

explanation: So true! Seeing constant suffering wears down even the strongest nurses. Taking care of your own mental health keeps you and your patients safe.

question: What is a major headache when trying to move medical supplies into a disaster zone?

options.A: Instantaneous electronic inventory updates everywhere
options.B: Damaged transport routes and broken infrastructure
options.C: Too many delivery trucks crowding the roads
options.D: Excessive amounts of clean storage space

explanation: You got it! When bridges collapse and roads are blocked with debris, getting medical boxes delivered becomes an extreme logistical puzzle.

question: Why do nurses need to track daily medication use closely in a field clinic?

options.A: To calculate daily hospital profits for insurance
options.B: To keep pharmacy staff busy with paperwork
options.C: To predict shortages and reorder supplies before running out
options.D: To prove to patients that drugs are expensive

explanation: Smart nursing! Keeping an eye on daily counts helps you spot when you're running low so you can reorder life-saving items ahead of time.

question: What is a crucial nursing duty BEFORE transferring a stabilized disaster victim to another hospital?

options.A: Remove all wound dressings for final inspection
options.B: Discontinue all intravenous fluids to save equipment
options.C: Wait for family members to sign financial clearance
options.D: Ensure secure lines, stable vitals, and handover notes

explanation: Spot on! Before they roll out, make sure their IV lines are secure, vitals are stable, and the receiving team has clear notes to continue good care.

question: Why is clear documentation so important during patient transfers in a disaster?

options.A: It prevents the ambulance driver from getting lost
options.B: It informs the receiving team of treatments already given
options.C: It guarantees the patient will recover faster
options.D: It serves as a legal ticket for free transport

explanation: Great job! Good handover notes stop medication errors and make sure the next team knows exactly what you've already done for the patient.

question: Which ethical rule guides how resources are shared when supplies are very scarce during a disaster?

options.A: Giving the newest supplies only to wealthy donors
options.B: Treating every person strictly on a first-come, first-served basis
options.C: Justice and doing the greatest good for the greatest number
options.D: Refusing care until formal legal contracts are signed

explanation: You've got it! In mass disasters, we shift from treating just one person to figuring out how to do the greatest good for the whole community fairly.

question: What makes ethical choices so emotionally heavy for nurses during a major disaster?

options.A: Having to ration scarce life-saving resources among many needy patients
options.B: Having too many modern medical machines to choose from
options.C: Working in fully air-conditioned and quiet field offices
options.D: Patients having unlimited time to discuss treatment options

explanation: So true. Deciding who gets scarce life-saving care when there isn't enough to go around is one of the hardest emotional burdens a nurse can carry.
